name: Illusions of the Desert
description: Chanek Jones is back, helping his long-lost relative Indiana Jones, to find a secret treasure in a maze buried below a desert full of illusions. The map of the labyrinth forms a tree with $$$n$$$ rooms numbered from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$ and $$$n - 1$$$ tunnels connecting them such that it is possible to travel between each pair of rooms through several tunnels. The $$$i$$$-th room ($$$1 \leq i \leq n$$$) has $$$a_i$$$ illusion rate. To go from the $$$x$$$-th room to the $$$y$$$-th room, there must exist a tunnel between $$$x$$$ and $$$y$$$, and it takes $$$\max(|a_x + a_y|, |a_x - a_y|)$$$ energy. $$$|z|$$$ denotes the absolute value of $$$z$$$. To prevent grave robbers, the maze can change the illusion rate of any room in it. Chanek and Indiana would ask $$$q$$$ queries. There are two types of queries to be done: $$$1\ u\ c$$$ — The illusion rate of the $$$x$$$-th room is changed to $$$c$$$ ($$$1 \leq u \leq n$$$, $$$0 \leq |c| \leq 10^9$$$). $$$2\ u\ v$$$ — Chanek and Indiana ask you the minimum sum of energy needed to take the secret treasure at room $$$v$$$ if they are initially at room $$$u$$$ ($$$1 \leq u, v \leq n$$$). Help them, so you can get a portion of the treasure!
input_specification: The first line contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$q$$$ ($$$2 \leq n \leq 10^5$$$, $$$1 \leq q \leq 10^5$$$) — the number of rooms in the maze and the number of queries. The second line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$$$ ($$$0 \leq |a_i| \leq 10^9$$$) — inital illusion rate of each room. The $$$i$$$-th of the next $$$n-1$$$ lines contains two integers $$$s_i$$$ and $$$t_i$$$ ($$$1 \leq s_i, t_i \leq n$$$), meaning there is a tunnel connecting $$$s_i$$$-th room and $$$t_i$$$-th room. The given edges form a tree. The next $$$q$$$ lines contain the query as described. The given queries are valid.
output_specification: For each type $$$2$$$ query, output a line containing an integer — the minimum sum of energy needed for Chanek and Indiana to take the secret treasure.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1575I — Illusions of the Desert [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
